hook: Nick Frosst studied computer science and cognitive science at the University of Toronto, working with researchers including John Tsotsos, Sanja Fidler and Jimmy Ba. He became the first employee of Geoffrey Hinton's Google Brain lab in Toronto, where he spent three years researching capsule networks, adversarial examples and model explainability. During that time he co-authored "Dynamic Routing Between Capsules" with Sara Sabour and Geoffrey Hinton, a widely cited paper proposing an alternative to standard convolutional pooling. In 2019 he left Google to co-found Cohere with Aidan Gomez and Ivan Zhang, building an enterprise-focused large language model company. Alongside his machine learning career, Frosst is also an active musician.
name: Nick Frosst
moniker: Co-founder of Cohere, capsule networks researcher

reading.body:
Nick Frosst moved from foundational deep learning research to building enterprise AI infrastructure, tracing a path from capsule network theory to large language model commercialization.

Frosst's work at Google Brain Toronto positioned him to see what pooling layers discard from convolutional networks: spatial relationships that capsule networks could preserve. This architectural research, published in 2017, explored how neural networks encode information rather than accepting the standard approach. When he co-founded Cohere two years later, he applied that research sensibility to a different problem: making large language models accessible to enterprises rather than a small set of API providers.

The timing matters for AI's infrastructure constraints. Frosst entered deep learning research when GPUs were becoming practical for training, worked through the period when scaling drove empirical gains, and started a company precisely when LLM inference costs became a business problem for customers. His trajectory shows how architectural research and commercialization can align, though the data does not reveal whether Cohere's technical strategy drew explicitly from capsule network insights or pursued a separate path.

What this does not show is why he chose Toronto for both ventures, or how his research team's choices differed from other LLM providers on the compute and power questions that shape AI's growth today.
